claim: MOF is responsible for the majority of H4K16 acetylation in mammals.
source: MOF is also responsible for the majority of H4K16 acetylation (Smith et al., 2005; Taipale et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to published work (Smith et al., 2005; Taipale et al., 2005)

claim: MOF is essential for mammalian embryonic development.
source: MOF is essential for mammalian embryonic development and unlike the male-specific lethality in Drosophila, deletion of Mof in mice is lethal for both sexes (Gupta et al., 2008; Thomas et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to published work (Gupta et al., 2008; Thomas et al., 2008)

claim: Deletion of Mof in mice is lethal for both sexes.
source: MOF is essential for mammalian embryonic development and unlike the male-specific lethality in Drosophila, deletion of Mof in mice is lethal for both sexes (Gupta et al., 2008; Thomas et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to published work (Gupta et al., 2008; Thomas et al., 2008)

claim: Mammalian MOF is critical for physiological nuclear architecture.
source: More specifically, mammalian MOF is critical for physiological nuclear architecture (Thomas et al., 2008), DNA damage repair (Gupta et al., 2008), maintenance of stem cell pluripotency (Li et al., 2012), differentiation of T cells (Gupta et al., 2013), and survival of post-mitotic Purkinje cells (Kumar et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to published work (Thomas et al., 2008)

claim: Mammalian MOF is critical for DNA damage repair.
source: More specifically, mammalian MOF is critical for physiological nuclear architecture (Thomas et al., 2008), DNA damage repair (Gupta et al., 2008), maintenance of stem cell pluripotency (Li et al., 2012), differentiation of T cells (Gupta et al., 2013), and survival of post-mitotic Purkinje cells (Kumar et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to published work (Gupta et al., 2008)

claim: Mammalian MOF is critical for maintenance of stem cell pluripotency.
source: More specifically, mammalian MOF is critical for physiological nuclear architecture (Thomas et al., 2008), DNA damage repair (Gupta et al., 2008), maintenance of stem cell pluripotency (Li et al., 2012), differentiation of T cells (Gupta et al., 2013), and survival of post-mitotic Purkinje cells (Kumar et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to published work (Li et al., 2012)

claim: Mammalian MOF is critical for differentiation of T cells.
source: More specifically, mammalian MOF is critical for physiological nuclear architecture (Thomas et al., 2008), DNA damage repair (Gupta et al., 2008), maintenance of stem cell pluripotency (Li et al., 2012), differentiation of T cells (Gupta et al., 2013), and survival of post-mitotic Purkinje cells (Kumar et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to published work (Gupta et al., 2013)

claim: Mammalian MOF is critical for survival of post-mitotic Purkinje cells.
source: More specifically, mammalian MOF is critical for physiological nuclear architecture (Thomas et al., 2008), DNA damage repair (Gupta et al., 2008), maintenance of stem cell pluripotency (Li et al., 2012), differentiation of T cells (Gupta et al., 2013), and survival of post-mitotic Purkinje cells (Kumar et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to published work (Kumar et al., 2011)

claim: Mutations of KANSL1 cause the core phenotype of the 17q21.31 microdeletion syndrome.
source: Nevertheless, the individual complex members appear to have important functions in vivo as mutations of the NSL complex member KANSL1 cause the core phenotype of the 17q21.31 microdeletion syndrome (Koolen et al., 2012; Zollino et al., 2012) and are common amongst patients with both Down syndrome and myeloid leukemia (Yoshida et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to published work (Koolen et al., 2012; Zollino et al., 2012)

claim: KANSL1 mutations are common amongst patients with both Down syndrome and myeloid leukemia.
source: Nevertheless, the individual complex members appear to have important functions in vivo as mutations of the NSL complex member KANSL1 cause the core phenotype of the 17q21.31 microdeletion syndrome (Koolen et al., 2012; Zollino et al., 2012) and are common amongst patients with both Down syndrome and myeloid leukemia (Yoshida et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to published work (Yoshida et al., 2013)

claim: PHF20 associates with methylated Lys370 and Lys382 of p53.
source: Another NSL-associated protein, PHF20 has been shown to associate with methylated Lys370 and Lys382 of p53 (Cui et al., 2012) and to be required for somatic cell reprogramming (Zhao et al., 2013a).
evidence: Supported by citation to published work (Cui et al., 2012)

claim: PHF20 is required for somatic cell reprogramming.
source: Another NSL-associated protein, PHF20 has been shown to associate with methylated Lys370 and Lys382 of p53 (Cui et al., 2012) and to be required for somatic cell reprogramming (Zhao et al., 2013a).
evidence: Supported by citation to published work (Zhao et al., 2013a)

claim: WDR5 is an essential regulator of the core transcription network in embryonic stem cells.
source: WDR5 was shown to be an essential regulator of the core transcription network in embryonic stem cells (Ang et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to published work (Ang et al., 2011)

claim: The mammalian counterpart of Drosophila MSL2 has the capacity to ubiquitylate p53.
source: The mammalian counterpart of Drosophila MSL2 was shown to have the capacity to ubiquitylate p53 (Kruse and Gu, 2009) and lysine 34 of histone 2B (Wu et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to published work (Kruse and Gu, 2009)

claim: The mammalian counterpart of Drosophila MSL2 has the capacity to ubiquitylate lysine 34 of histone 2B.
source: The mammalian counterpart of Drosophila MSL2 was shown to have the capacity to ubiquitylate p53 (Kruse and Gu, 2009) and lysine 34 of histone 2B (Wu et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to published work (Wu et al., 2011)

claim: KANSL1 and KANSL3 protein levels remained unchanged during differentiation from ESCs to NPCs.
source: Interestingly, MSL and NSL complex members showed distinct RNA and protein dynamics during the process of differentiation: KANSL1 and KANSL3 protein levels remained unchanged, whereas MSL1, MSL2 and MOF became more abundant in NPCs accompanied by increased H4K16 acetylation (H4K16ac) (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B

claim: MSL1, MSL2 and MOF became more abundant in NPCs compared to ESCs.
source: Interestingly, MSL and NSL complex members showed distinct RNA and protein dynamics during the process of differentiation: KANSL1 and KANSL3 protein levels remained unchanged, whereas MSL1, MSL2 and MOF became more abundant in NPCs accompanied by increased H4K16 acetylation (H4K16ac) (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B

claim: H4K16 acetylation increased during differentiation from ESCs to NPCs.
source: Interestingly, MSL and NSL complex members showed distinct RNA and protein dynamics during the process of differentiation: KANSL1 and KANSL3 protein levels remained unchanged, whereas MSL1, MSL2 and MOF became more abundant in NPCs accompanied by increased H4K16 acetylation (H4K16ac) (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B

claim: Unsupervised clustering identified five distinct groups of binding for MOF, MSL and NSL proteins in ESCs and NPCs.
source: We applied unsupervised clustering on the union of peaks from all ChIP-seq samples and thereby identified five distinct groups of binding for MOF, MSL and NSL proteins in ESCs and NPCs.
evidence: Supported by experimental data and analysis shown in Figure 2

claim: Three large clusters of binding sites encompassed regions where at least 1 of the investigated proteins was present both in ESCs and NPCs.
source: As shown in Figure 2, three large clusters of binding sites encompassed regions, where at least 1 of the investigated proteins was present both in ESCs and NPCs (clusters A, B and C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2

claim: The binding sites of clusters A and B predominantly overlapped with annotated transcription start sites (TSS).
source: The binding sites of clusters A and B predominantly overlapped with annotated transcription start sites (TSS) in contrast to the regions that were bound exclusively in ESCs, which tended to contain inter- and intragenic regions (clusters D and E, Figure 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2

claim: Regions bound exclusively in ESCs tended to contain inter- and intragenic regions.
source: The binding sites of clusters A and B predominantly overlapped with annotated transcription start sites (TSS) in contrast to the regions that were bound exclusively in ESCs, which tended to contain inter- and intragenic regions (clusters D and E, Figure 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2

claim: Approximately 80% of all MOF peaks displayed strong KANSL3 and MCRS1 signals.
source: We found surprisingly few regions where MOF associated primarily with MSL complex members. Instead, approximately 80% of all MOF peaks displayed strong KANSL3 and MCRS1 signals (cluster B, see Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), suggesting a predominant role of the NSL complex among MOF-associated complexes and a more specific role for the MSL complex at subsets of promoters and numerous intergenic and intronic regions.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B

claim: 8947 TSSs overlapped with ChIP-seq peaks of KANSL3 and/or MCRS1 in ESCs.
source: We identified 8947 TSSs overlapping with ChIP-seq peaks of KANSL3 and/or MCRS1 in ESCs that encompassed virtually all MOF- and MSL-bound TSSs (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B

claim: 99% of TSSs overlapping with MOF peaks in NPCs showed significant enrichments of KANSL3.
source: This pattern did not change substantially in NPCs where TSSs overlapping with MOF peaks almost always (99%) showed significant enrichments of KANSL3 and in 35% of the cases additionally contained a peak of MSL2 (Figure 3B, middle panel).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B

claim: 35% of TSSs overlapping with MOF peaks in NPCs additionally contained a peak of MSL2.
source: This pattern did not change substantially in NPCs where TSSs overlapping with MOF peaks almost always (99%) showed significant enrichments of KANSL3 and in 35% of the cases additionally contained a peak of MSL2 (Figure 3B, middle panel).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B

claim: All ChIPed proteins preferably bound to the promoters of active genes.
source: We next generated RNA-seq data for ESCs and NPCs, determined genes that were expressed in both cell types (FPKM >4) and found that all ChIPed proteins preferably bound to the promoters of active genes (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C

claim: In ESCs, genes whose TSSs were bound by members of both complexes showed higher median expression values than genes bound by only one complex.
source: Interestingly, in ESCs, genes whose TSSs were bound by members of both complexes showed higher median expression values than genes bound by only one complex (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B

claim: The promoters of all target gene groups were enriched for motifs associated with broad, non-cell-type-specific expression such as ELK1, YY1, CREB, and E2F.
source: Consistently, the promoters of all target gene groups were enriched for motifs associated with broad, non-cell-type-specific expression such as ELK1, YY1, CREB, and E2F (Xie et al., 2005; Farre et al., 2007) and showed profound enrichments of CpG islands (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D), which is indicative of housekeeping genes (Landolin et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D and citations (Xie et al., 2005; Farre et al., 2007)

claim: The promoters of all target gene groups showed profound enrichments of CpG islands.
source: Consistently, the promoters of all target gene groups were enriched for motifs associated with broad, non-cell-type-specific expression such as ELK1, YY1, CREB, and E2F (Xie et al., 2005; Farre et al., 2007) and showed profound enrichments of CpG islands (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D), which is indicative of housekeeping genes (Landolin et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D and citation (Landolin et al., 2010)

claim: MOF- or KANSL3-depleted cells showed more severe proliferation defects than MSL1- and MSL2-depleted cells.
source: Interestingly, MOF- or KANSL3-depleted cells showed more severe proliferation defects than MSL1- and MSL2-depleted cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3B

claim: There was a striking overlap between the differential expression of MSL1 and MSL2 knockdowns.
source: We found a striking overlap between the differential expression of MSL1 and MSL2 knockdowns and a higher resemblance of MOF-dependent differential expression to that of KANSL3-depletion (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E

claim: MOF-dependent differential expression showed higher resemblance to that of KANSL3-depletion than to MSL1 or MSL2 knockdowns.
source: We found a striking overlap between the differential expression of MSL1 and MSL2 knockdowns and a higher resemblance of MOF-dependent differential expression to that of KANSL3-depletion (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E

claim: Genes identified as TSS-bound in ChIP-seq samples tended to be downregulated in all four knockdowns in comparison to untargeted genes.
source: When we specifically focused on genes that we had identified as TSS-bound in our ChIP-seq samples, we found that their transcripts tended to be downregulated in all four knockdowns in comparison to untargeted genes which showed higher fractions of upregulation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F

claim: Markedly reduced bulk H4K16 acetylation was detected in MSL1- and MOF-depleted cells.
source: Turning to the assessment of protein levels in shRNA-treated cells, we detected markedly reduced bulk H4K16 acetylation in MSL1- and MOF-depleted cells and only slight reduction upon KANSL3-depletion.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G

claim: Only slight reduction of bulk H4K16 acetylation was detected upon KANSL3-depletion.
source: Turning to the assessment of protein levels in shRNA-treated cells, we detected markedly reduced bulk H4K16 acetylation in MSL1- and MOF-depleted cells and only slight reduction upon KANSL3-depletion.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G

claim: MSL1-depletion affected the levels of MSL2 but not of NSL complex members.
source: In addition, we found that MSL1-depletion affected the levels of MSL2 but not of NSL complex members while the depletion of KANSL3 moderately decreased protein levels for both complexes (Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G

claim: Depletion of KANSL3 moderately decreased protein levels for both MSL and NSL complexes.
source: In addition, we found that MSL1-depletion affected the levels of MSL2 but not of NSL complex members while the depletion of KANSL3 moderately decreased protein levels for both complexes (Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G

claim: MSL1 and KANSL3 do not require the presence of MOF to bind to gene promoters.
source: ChIP-qPCR assays in MOF-depleted cells revealed that MSL1 and KANSL3 do not require the presence of MOF to bind to gene promoters, which is in agreement with previous observations in D. melanogaster (Hallacli et al., 2012; Figure 3—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4C and citation (Hallacli et al., 2012)

claim: MSL2, MCRS1, and KANSL3 were predominantly enriched within introns and intergenic regions in ESC-specific binding sites.
source: In addition to promoter-proximal binding, where both the MSL and NSL complex tend to (co-)occur constitutively in ESCs and NPCs, we identified a large proportion of binding sites where the proteins were present in a dynamic fashion, that is their binding was observed only in ESCs but not in NPCs (Figure 2, clusters D and E). In contrast to the binding mode represented by clusters A and B (Figure 2), here MSL2, MCRS1, and KANSL3 were predominantly enriched within introns and intergenic regions that underwent significant CpG methylation upon differentiation (e.g., from median 50% CpG methylation in ESCs to more than 80% in NPCs for cluster D; bisulfite sequencing data from Stadler et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2 and citation (Stadler et al., 2011)

claim: ESC-specific binding sites underwent significant CpG methylation upon differentiation.
source: In contrast to the binding mode represented by clusters A and B (Figure 2), here MSL2, MCRS1, and KANSL3 were predominantly enriched within introns and intergenic regions that underwent significant CpG methylation upon differentiation (e.g., from median 50% CpG methylation in ESCs to more than 80% in NPCs for cluster D; bisulfite sequencing data from Stadler et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citation (Stadler et al., 2011)

claim: The regions of cluster D showed highly localized enrichments of DNase hypersensitivity sites, RNA Polymerase II, p300, H3K4me1, and H3K27ac in ESCs.
source: In addition, the regions of cluster D and, to a lesser extent the MSL1-rich cluster E (Figure 2), showed highly localized enrichments of DNase hypersensitivity sites (DNase HS), RNA Polymerase II (Pol II), p300, methylation of histone 3 on lysine 4 (H3K4me1), and acetylation of histone 3 on lysine 27 (H3K27ac) in ESCs (Figure 4A), which are characteristic features of enhancer regions.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A

claim: MSL2, KANSL3 and MCRS1, but not MOF and MSL1, showed profound enrichments for active and poised ESC enhancers.
source: Interestingly, MSL2, KANSL3 and MCRS1, but not MOF and MSL1, showed profound enrichments for active and poised ESC enhancers (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) as well as along the regions of super enhancers that have been described as being particularly important for maintenance of cell identity (Whyte et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and citation (Whyte et al., 2013)

claim: The signals of MSL2 and KANSL3 were specific for ESC enhancers and wide-spread along super enhancer regions.
source: The signals of MSL2 and KANSL3 were specific for ESC enhancers and wide-spread along super enhancer regions (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B,C

claim: Enhancers overlapping with MSL2 ChIP-seq peaks tended to show lower KANSL3 enrichments and vice versa.
source: We noted that enhancers overlapping with MSL2 ChIP-seq peaks tended to show lower KANSL3 enrichments and vice versa, implying that MSL2 and KANSL3 preferred different enhancer regions (heatmaps in Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B

claim: MOF was not enriched at super enhancers.
source: MOF was not enriched at super enhancers and generally, its binding to TSS-distal sites was much less pronounced than to gene promoters (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, 1C, Figure 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, 1C, Figure 2

claim: 87% of TSS-distal MOF peak regions overlapped with either KANSL3 or MSL2.
source: Like for TSS-specific binding, MOF was not alone (87% of TSS-distal MOF peak regions overlapped with either KANSL3 or MSL2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data analysis

claim: Approximately 81% of cluster C regions had solitary MSL2 enrichments without significant signals of any of the other ChIPed proteins.
source: Approximately, 81% of these cluster C regions had solitary MSL2 enrichments without significant signals of any of the other ChIPed proteins.
evidence: Supported by experimental data analysis

claim: Solitary MSL2 binding sites increased in number and binding strength upon differentiation to NPCs.
source: Interestingly, these MSL2 binding sites increased in number and binding strength upon differentiation to NPCs (829 solitary MSL2 peaks in ESCs compared to 3635 in NPCs).
evidence: Supported by experimental data analysis

claim: A (CAGA)n motif was obtained when searching the unique MSL2 binding sites for DNA motifs.
source: When we searched the unique MSL2 binding sites for DNA motifs, we obtained a (CAGA)n motif (Figure 4—figure supplement 3B) that was previously described as a binding site for SMAD3, a transcription factor that translates the TGF-beta receptor response into gene expression regulation (Zawel et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3B and citation (Zawel et al., 1998)

claim: All five tested regions located near genes related to pluripotency and self-renewal showed strong transcriptional enhancement in ESCs, but not in NPCs or 3T3 cells.
source: Using luciferase reporter constructs, we found strong transcriptional enhancement for all tested regions in ESCs, but not in NPCs or 3T3 cells which correlated with the presence of MSL2 and/or KANSL3 and MCRS1 in ESCs only (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 4A

claim: The numbers of TSS-distal targets of MSL1 or MSL2 that were significantly reduced in the respective shRNA-treatments were markedly larger than for genes where MSL1 or MSL2 bound to the promoter.
source: In fact, the numbers of TSS-distal targets of MSL1 or MSL2 that were significantly reduced in the respective shRNA-treatments were markedly larger than for genes where MSL1 or MSL2 bound to the promoter (compare Figure 3F with Figure 4—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F and Figure 4—figure supplement 4B

claim: The majority of enhancer regions associated with key pluripotency factors were strongly enriched for MSL2 and KANSL3.
source: While TSS-binding predominantly occurred at housekeeping genes, we noticed that the majority of enhancer regions associated with key pluripotency factors (e.g., SOX2, ESRRB, MYC, REX1, TBX3, NANOG) were strongly enriched for MSL2 and KANSL3.
evidence: Supported by experimental data analysis

claim: MOF- or KANSL3-depleted cells showed strongly reduced levels of NANOG, REX1, and ESRRB.
source: We thus assessed the effects of the protein depletions on pluripotency factors in ESCs and found strongly reduced levels of NANOG, REX1, and ESRRB in MOF- or KANSL3-depleted cells.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F

claim: The pluripotency factors remained almost unaffected in cells depleted of MSL1 or MSL2.
source: Surprisingly, the pluripotency factors remained almost unaffected in cells depleted of MSL1 or MSL2 (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F

claim: Decreased levels of alkaline phosphatase were observed in MOF- and KANSL3-, but not in MSL1- or MSL2-depleted cells.
source: These contrasting results were mirrored by decreased levels of alkaline phosphatase (AP) in MOF- and KANSL3-, but not in MSL1- or MSL2-depleted cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 4D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4D

claim: The XIC site with the strongest concomitant enrichments of MSL1, MSL2 and MOF was the major promoter (P2) of Tsix and its intronic minisatellite—DXPas34.
source: The XIC site with the strongest concomitant enrichments of MSL1, MSL2 and MOF was the major promoter (P2) of Tsix and its intronic minisatellite—DXPas34 (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A,B

claim: DXPas34 is a tandem repeat that serves as a binding platform for multiple transcription factors and contains bidirectional enhancing properties essential for the expression of Tsix.
source: DXPas34 is a well-characterized tandem repeat that serves as a binding platform for multiple transcription factors and contains bidirectional enhancing properties essential for the expression of Tsix, the antisense transcript of Xist (Debrand et al., 1999; Cohen et al., 2007; Donohoe et al., 2007; Navarro et al., 2010; Gontan et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to published work (Debrand et al., 1999; Cohen et al., 2007; Donohoe et al., 2007; Navarro et al., 2010; Gontan et al., 2012)

claim: DXPas34 deletion impairs the recruitment of Pol II and TFIIB to the major promoter of Tsix causing its downregulation.
source: In turn, DXPas34 deletion impairs the recruitment of Pol II and TFIIB to the major promoter of Tsix causing its downregulation (Vigneau et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to published work (Vigneau et al., 2006)

claim: MSL peaks were detected on the promoters, gene bodies and intronic regions of other key XIC regulators including Xist, Jpx, Tsx, and Rnf12.
source: In addition to the DXPas34 binding site, we detected MSL peaks on the promoters, gene bodies and intronic regions of other key XIC regulators including the genes of the long non-coding (lnc) RNAs Xist and Jpx. Additionally, we observed peaks upstream of the Tsx gene and both at the TSS and downstream of the Rnf12 gene (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A

claim: The XIC binding of MSL-MOF was specific to ESCs, as almost all enrichments were abolished upon differentiation.
source: The XIC binding of MSL-MOF was specific to ESCs, as almost all enrichments were abolished upon differentiation, except for some loci upstream of Xist where traces of binding could still be detected in NPCs (e.g., Ftx and Jpx TSS, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A

claim: The recruitment of MOF was almost completely abolished in both MSL1- and MSL2-depleted cells.
source: Interestingly, the recruitment of MOF was almost completely abolished in both MSL1- and MSL2-depleted cells, whereas the depletion of MOF had no effect on MSL1 and MSL2 binding to the Tsix major promoter and DXPas34 (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C

claim: The depletion of MOF had no effect on MSL1 and MSL2 binding to the Tsix major promoter and DXPas34.
source: Interestingly, the recruitment of MOF was almost completely abolished in both MSL1- and MSL2-depleted cells, whereas the depletion of MOF had no effect on MSL1 and MSL2 binding to the Tsix major promoter and DXPas34 (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C

claim: H4K16 acetylation ChIP signals were severely reduced in both MOF- and MSL2-depleted cells.
source: H4K16 acetylation ChIP signals were severely reduced in both MOF- and MSL2-depleted cells.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C

claim: MSL1 and MSL2 are together necessary and sufficient for the recruitment of MOF and for the deposition of H4K16 acetylation at DXPas34.
source: These results are in agreement with our global observations (Figure 3G, Figure 3—figure supplement 4C) and indicate that MSL1 and MSL2 are together necessary and sufficient for the recruitment of MOF and for the deposition of H4K16 acetylation at DXPas34.
evidence: Supported by experimental data and inference from results

claim: Only MSL1- and MSL2-, but not MOF-depletion led to pronounced downregulation of Tsix both in male and female ESCs.
source: Unexpectedly, only MSL1- and MSL2-, but not MOF-depletion led to pronounced downregulation of Tsix both in male and female ESCs (Figure 6A; note that in our RNA-seq data set for MSL2-depleted cells, Tsix was among the five most strongly downregulated genes).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A

claim: Downregulation of Tsix was accompanied by moderately elevated Xist RNA levels in MSL1- and MSL2-depleted ESCs.
source: Downregulation of Tsix was accompanied by moderately elevated Xist RNA levels in MSL1- and MSL2-depleted ESCs whereas depletion of MOF yielded the most pronounced (8–15-fold) upregulation of Xist without affecting Tsix.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A

claim: Depletion of MOF yielded the most pronounced (8–15-fold) upregulation of Xist without affecting Tsix.
source: Downregulation of Tsix was accompanied by moderately elevated Xist RNA levels in MSL1- and MSL2-depleted ESCs whereas depletion of MOF yielded the most pronounced (8–15-fold) upregulation of Xist without affecting Tsix.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A

claim: RNA-FISH confirmed global reduction and in many cases elimination of DXPas34 signals in MSL1- and MSL2-, but not in MOF-depleted cells.
source: The RNA-FISH confirmed the qPCR results as we observed global reduction and in many cases elimination of DXPas34 signals in MSL1- and MSL2-, but not in MOF-depleted cells (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–C

claim: The depletion of MOF (but not of MSL1 or MSL2) in female ESCs resulted in a significant decrease of transcript and protein levels of pluripotency factors that had previously been associated with Xist repression.
source: Like for MOF- and KANSL3-depletions in male ESCs (Figure 4F), the depletion of MOF (but not of MSL1 or MSL2) in female ESCs resulted in a significant decrease of transcript and protein levels of pluripotency factors that had previously been associated with Xist repression (e.g., NANOG and REX1; see Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1D

claim: The depletion of MSL2 led to significant downregulation of Ftx and Jpx genes whose promoters were bound by MSL1 and/or MSL2.
source: Only depletion of MSL2 led to significant downregulation of Ftx and Jpx genes whose promoters were bound by MSL1 and/or MSL2 (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1E

claim: Depletion of MOF led to moderate upregulation of Linx lncRNA.
source: On the other hand, depletion of MOF led to moderate upregulation of Linx lncRNA, which acts synergistically with Tsix (Nora et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citation (Nora et al., 2012)

claim: Neither the depletion of MSL1 and MSL2 nor the depletion of MOF significantly influenced protein levels of RNF12, YY1, or CTCF.
source: Neither the depletion of MSL1 and MSL2 nor the depletion of MOF significantly influenced protein levels of RNF12, YY1, or CTCF that are known regulators of the XIC (Figure 6D; Donohoe et al., 2007, 2009; Jonkers et al., 2009; Shin et al., 2010; Jeon and Lee, 2011).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D and citations (Donohoe et al., 2007, 2009; Jonkers et al., 2009; Shin et al., 2010; Jeon and Lee, 2011)

claim: The depletion of MSL2 led to significant reduction of REX1 ChIP signals across the DXPas34 locus.
source: Indeed, the depletion of MSL2 led to significant reduction of REX1 ChIP signals across the DXPas34 locus whereas the effect on YY1-targeting was less pronounced and restricted to the Tsix major promoter (P2) (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E

claim: The effect of MSL2 depletion on YY1-targeting was less pronounced and restricted to the Tsix major promoter (P2).
source: Indeed, the depletion of MSL2 led to significant reduction of REX1 ChIP signals across the DXPas34 locus whereas the effect on YY1-targeting was less pronounced and restricted to the Tsix major promoter (P2) (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E

claim: Accumulating Xist lncRNA and X-chromosomal coating was observed in a small fraction of MSL1- and MSL2-depleted female ESCs.
source: Interestingly, we observed accumulating Xist lncRNA and X-chromosomal coating in a small fraction of MSL1- and MSL2-depleted female ESCs (but not MOF-depleted cells; 4–5% of the cell population in shMsl1 and shMsl2 with comparison to 0.5% in scrambled control, see Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–C

claim: The induction of differentiation resulted in a stronger elevation of Xist RNA levels in MSL1- and MSL2-depleted cells in comparison to the scrambled control.
source: Consistent with our previous results, the induction of differentiation resulted in a stronger elevation of Xist RNA levels in MSL1- and MSL2-depleted cells in comparison to the scrambled control (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B

claim: All three knockdowns (MSL1, MSL2, MOF) resulted in enhanced Xist accumulation and X-chromosomal coating after 3 days of differentiation.
source: All three knockdowns resulted in enhanced Xist accumulation and X-chromosomal coating (63.1%, 61.1% and 50.6% of all counted cells in shMsl1-, shMsl2-, and shMof-treated ESCs, respectively, in comparison to scrambled control with 39.1% of counted cells; see Figure 7C,D and Figure 7—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C,D and Figure 7—figure supplement 2A,B

claim: MSL1- and MSL2-depleted differentiating cells contained numerous cells with two inactive X chromosomes.
source: Interestingly, we observed that MSL1- and MSL2-depleted differentiating cells contained numerous cells with two inactive X chromosomes.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7E

claim: The fraction of cells where both X chromosomes underwent XCI was approximately 10-fold higher in Msl1 and Msl2 knockdown compared to the scrambled control.
source: The fraction of cells where both X chromosomes underwent XCI was approximately 10-fold higher in Msl1 and Msl2 knockdown compared to the scrambled control (Figure 7E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7E

claim: The depletion of MSL proteins results in severe downregulation of Tsix transcription and enhanced accumulation of Xist during early differentiation.
source: Taken together, our data establishes MSL1 and MSL2 among the key regulators of Tsix transcription, as the depletion of MSL proteins results in severe downregulation of Tsix transcription and enhanced accumulation of Xist during early differentiation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data and inference from results

claim: The NSL complex has general, housekeeping functions whereas the MSL complex predominantly performs more specialized tasks.
source: We determined five basic modes of co-occurrence that revealed cell-type-specific as well as constitutive functions of the different proteins and support the notion that the NSL complex has general, housekeeping functions whereas the MSL complex predominantly performs more specialized tasks.
evidence: Supported by experimental data and inference from results

claim: MOF and its associated proteins are involved in gene expression regulation via targeting the promoters of housekeeping genes in a cell-type-independent manner.
source: We show that MOF and its associated proteins are involved in gene expression regulation via different means: first, they all target the promoters of housekeeping genes in a cell-type-independent manner and second, members of both complexes occupy different sets of ESC-specific enhancers that are essential for the maintenance of stem cell identity.
evidence: Supported by experimental data and inference from results

claim: Members of both MSL and NSL complexes occupy different sets of ESC-specific enhancers that are essential for the maintenance of stem cell identity.
source: We show that MOF and its associated proteins are involved in gene expression regulation via different means: first, they all target the promoters of housekeeping genes in a cell-type-independent manner and second, members of both complexes occupy different sets of ESC-specific enhancers that are essential for the maintenance of stem cell identity.
evidence: Supported by experimental data and inference from results

claim: Both MSL and NSL complexes contribute to the repression of X inactivation in ESCs via different means.
source: We demonstrate the distinct and novel functions carried out by the MOF-associated complex members by revealing that both complexes contribute to the repression of X inactivation in ESCs via different means: While we establish the MSL complex as a direct regulator of Tsix, MOF and the NSL complex play an important role in the maintenance of pluripotency factors (Figure 8).

claim: The MSL complex is a direct regulator of Tsix.

evidence: Supported by experimental data and inference from results shown in Figure 8

claim: MOF and the NSL complex play an important role in the maintenance of pluripotency factors.

claim: MSL1 is the major enhancer of MOF's H4K16 acetylation activity.
source: This is consistent with previous reports that indicate MSL1 as the major enhancer of MOF's H4K16 acetylation (Kadlec et al., 2011) and demonstrate relaxed substrate specificity for the NSL complex (Zhao et al., 2013b).

claim: The NSL complex has relaxed substrate specificity.
source: This is consistent with previous reports that indicate MSL1 as the major enhancer of MOF's H4K16 acetylation (Kadlec et al., 2011) and demonstrate relaxed substrate specificity for the NSL complex (Zhao et al., 2013b).

claim: MOF is vital for the maintenance of pluripotency.
source: These results support the recent finding that MOF is vital for the maintenance of pluripotency (Li et al., 2012), but we furthermore show that this is an NSL- and not MSL-related function of MOF independent of H4K16 acetylation deposition.
evidence: Supported by citation to published work (Li et al., 2012)

claim: The maintenance of pluripotency by MOF is an NSL- and not MSL-related function of MOF independent of H4K16 acetylation deposition.

claim: The Drosophila homologue of KANSL3 can directly activate transcription in vitro.
source: Both proteins are in principle capable of supporting transcription: the Drosophila homologue of KANSL3 can directly activate transcription in vitro (Raja et al., 2010) and human MSL2 acts as an E3 ubiquitin ligase at lysine 34 of H2B (H2BK34ub) (Wu et al., 2011), which has been suggested to promote methylation of H3K4, and thus gene expression (Wu et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to published work (Raja et al., 2010)

claim: In undifferentiated ESCs, where pluripotency factors are highly abundant, even severe downregulation of Tsix, or Tsix-deletion has almost no effect on Xist transcription.
source: Previous studies demonstrated that in undifferentiated ESCs, where pluripotency factors are highly abundant, even severe downregulation of Tsix, or Tsix-deletion has almost no effect on Xist transcription (Morey et al., 2001; Navarro et al., 2005; Nesterova et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to published work (Morey et al., 2001; Navarro et al., 2005; Nesterova et al., 2011)

claim: The repressive potential of Tsix on Xist accumulation and the role of Tsix and the DXPas34 locus in the process of counting and choice of XCI becomes fully apparent during early stages of differentiation.

evidence: Supported by citations to published work (Lee, 2005; Vigneau et al., 2006; Rougeulle and Avner, 2004)
